rv.q: Even so, “Master Class” remains a diverting and at times juicily amusing vehicle for an actress capable of bottling a prima donna’s blunt-force charisma.

Well, that is who she was, as we learn from a playwright who knows whereof he speaks and from Daly’s triumphant portrayal of her.
Even if the play is essentially a monologue mixed with some opera selections, it makes for a thrilling ride and is one of McNally's most compelling works.
She is a woman who appears to command the world - played here by a woman who clearly commands a room.
Tyne Daly's Maria Callas is a force of nature, commanding the stage with the kind of theatrical authority that makes you forget you're watching a performance.
Tyne Daly has made it her own with a performance that's both commanding and deeply moving.
But by Act Two, when Maria is more focused on actually transforming her students at any cost, Tyne is earthy, sharp, bitchy, and moving.

Manhattan Theatre Club has imported this production of 'Master Class' from the Kennedy Center's 2010 tribute to playwright Terrence McNally, where it was a sizeable hit. Spruced up with some recasting and featuring an improved turn from star Tyne Daly, the show should repeat its D.C. success.
Even for those who know nothing about the opera or Callas, “Master Class” is an engaging and informative couple of hours with a formidable teacher.
McNally's well-crafted, quip-filled drama — which depicts Callas teaching at Juilliard, circa 1971 — is less a biography and more a love letter to La Divina.
Daly, a forceful, convincingly complex presence in the coaching scenes, seems uncertain and unfocussed in the reveries (where Stephen Wadsworth's scattershot staging doesn't help).
Daly delivers a commanding performance that is a master class all by itself.
Her ego rises above her generosity of spirit making her Callas an unforgettable monster.
